codecs.note: Base91z 0.4.x, JSON-safe alphabet with typed segments

codecs.name: base91z (auto)
codecs.note: Base91z choosing its own compression, at its own default level

balanced.label: Balanced
balanced.note: Everything the corpus holds, counted evenly. The default, and the one to distrust: no real system's traffic looks like this.

binary.label: Binary data
binary.note: Container formats, executables, fonts, images, archives. No text structure to exploit, but plenty of internal redundancy for a compressor to find.

dense_problem_chars.label: Many problematic characters
dense_problem_chars.note: Text so peppered with untransportable bytes that escaping it in place would be worse than encoding it outright. Where a binary-to-text encoding stops being a fallback and becomes the obvious choice.

incompressible.label: Compressed or random data
incompressible.note: Session identifiers, ciphertext, already-compressed blobs, and pure noise. A compression stage in front of the encoder earns nothing here, so the encoding is on its own -- and this is exactly the traffic that reaches for one.

mixed_content.label: Mixed content
mixed_content.note: One envelope carrying several kinds of thing at once: structured text, source, a binary attachment. What a real message tends to hold, and the case where an encoding cannot specialise its way out.

sparse_problem_chars.label: A few problematic characters
sparse_problem_chars.note: Text that is almost all plain ASCII with the occasional byte that breaks it -- a log line with a stray control character, a field with one byte of raw UTF-8 gone wrong. The case where escaping in place might still have been cheaper, and the report should be able to say whether it was.
